articles.title: Why Ozempic Weight Loss Stalls for Some People but Not Others
articles.dek: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy help some people lose remarkable amounts of weight while others see disappointing results?
paragraphs: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy help some people lose remarkable amounts of weight while others see disappointing results?
Scientists are investigating whether the body’s natural tendency to conserve energy during weight loss could be an overlooked piece of the puzzle.

Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite, and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.

Research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite.

These medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time.
We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially important piece in a complex puzzle.

Research has shown that semaglutide medications can improve quality of life, blood markers such as sugar and cholesterol, strength, and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work.

We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age, and sex.

Energy metabolism may also be an important piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym, and the everyday act of digesting food.

When we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis .
Think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau.

Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an important role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories.

Researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term.

We published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization . We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive.

articles.title: The avian champions of long-distance migration keep surprising scientists
articles.dek: "The whole story began with an extinct bird from Hispaniola," said Min Zhao, a former postdoctoral associate at the Florida Museum of Natural History (now a postdoctoral…
paragraphs: "The whole story began with an extinct bird from Hispaniola," said Min Zhao, a former postdoctoral associate at the Florida Museum of Natural History (now a postdoctoral researcher at Uppsala University).
The bird in question was identified as a woodcock in 2015 based on several fossils excavated by Florida Museum researchers in 1984 from a Haitian cave on the island of Hispaniola.

Woodcocks are medium-sized birds with long, slightly curved beaks that appear to protrude from their necks and a bouncy back-and-forth gait that looks like a funky, two-step dance number. Scientists think this comic method of locomotion may mimic the vibrations made by falling rain, which is a cue for earthworms to move upward before the soil becomes waterlogged and they drown. Instead, vertically migrating earthworms encounter the slender bill of the woodcock.

In a new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , Florida Museum researchers sequenced ancient DNA from the fossil specimens and showed that what was thought to be a woodcock is actually a snipe.

That in itself isn't very surprising. Woodcocks and snipes are each other's closest relatives, having diverged from a common ancestor about 25 million years ago . To the untrained eye, they can look nearly identical. The misidentified snipe also had short wings and big legs—two common traits in island birds—compared with what scientists now know are its closest relatives.

But the combined efforts of the research group reveal a broader story about migration and evolution in a group of birds famous for flying nonstop from the high latitudes of one hemisphere to those of the other.

"Shorebirds are the ultimate long-distance migrants," said study coauthor David Steadman, the emeritus curator of ornithology at the Florida Museum. "It's common for shorebirds to nest up in the Arctic tundra and winter in South America. There was recently a bristle-thighed curlew that was radio-tagged and showed up in New Zealand after flying 10,000 km (6,200 miles) without stopping."

Like curlews, woodcocks and snipes also travel long distances, but unlike curlews and most other shorebirds, they also include several species whose ancestors opted out of migration and permanently settled down on islands. There are eight living species of woodcock, for example, and six of them are endemic to islands.

"Some people argue that it's their migratory propensity that has led them to colonize islands. But there are a lot of migrant shorebirds that travel long distances. Woodcocks and snipes are the only ones setting up resident populations on islands. They've radiated on islands in the Caribbean, Japan, Indonesia, the western Pacific and the greater New Zealand area," Steadman said.

Intrigued by the results of the ancient DNA analysis, Steadman and his colleagues wanted to see if they could learn more about how woodcocks and snipes evolved and radiated around the world over the last quarter-million years.

The study's coauthors collected small tissue samples from specimens in museums across the country for all but one of the 29 extant woodcock and snipe species. Jessica Oswald, a postdoctoral researcher then working at the Florida Museum of Natural History, extracted and sequenced DNA from these samples and—with help from coauthor Brian Stucky—managed to do so for the Hispaniolan fossils as well. She also included DNA from one additional extinct species, the South Island snipe, which disappeared in 1964 following the human-mediated introduction of black rats to South and Stewart islands in New Zealand.

They added the ages of shorebird fossils to their DNA data and analyzed both together to produce a time-calibrated phylogeny, or what is essentially the species-level equivalent of a family tree with dates added to it.

Several of the authors have conducted similar studies in the past. Coauthor Oswald extracted ancient DNA from numerous fossil specimens while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum.

articles.title: Repeated bending strengthens sugar-based hydrogel instead of wearing it down

paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

Most materials get weaker with use. But a team led by Chenfeng Ke, a professor of chemistry in Arts & Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis, has created a polymer that defies the usual laws of wear and tear.

"Our smart material actually gets stronger the more it's bent and strained," Ke said. "It has properties we have never seen before. It can remember, adapt, learn and grow. We're excited to think about the possible applications."
The breakthrough was described in a study published online in Nature Materials . Co-authors include graduate students Yufei Chen and Mingliang Bai and postdoctoral researcher Dan Zheng.

The patented polymer, created in Ke's lab with compatibility for 3D printing, is made from a biodegradable blend of sugar crystals and polyethylene glycol, a compound often used in laxatives and other health products. The mixture forms a hydrogel, a flexible material that can absorb and retain large amounts of water.

In tests, Ke and his team applied the material to a flexible, knee-like joint. "We bent it 10,000 times, and the material performed just as we predicted," Ke said. "The polymers in the hydrogel become more uniform and organized, making it stronger in exactly the places where the strain is happening."

The smart material owes its strength and adaptability to cyclodextrin, a sugar-based compound that forms ring-shaped structures. When the polymer is stretched or bent, these rings slide into position to reinforce the areas under strain. "These moving rings are critical to the structural design," Ke said.

In many ways, the material mimics biological materials in the human body, including collagen, a protein that gives skin its strength and elasticity. "Some of the most impressive smart materials are found in biology," Ke said. "We used nature for inspiration."
Ke believes the polymer could have medical applications, particularly in protecting and repairing tissues.

"Because it's made of sugar and polyethylene glycol, it's completely compatible with biological tissues," Ke said. "We expect this material to attract interest from surgeons or orthopedic medical device companies who are looking for new approaches."

For example, the material could be used to support artificial joints or to repair damaged tissues. In either case, areas that aren't subjected to stress or strain would remain soft and pliable. "If you're putting material into a body, you don't necessarily want it to be completely rigid," Ke said. "The material gets stronger only where it's needed."
Ke is a chemist, not an orthopedist or medical device specialist, and he acknowledges that other experts may recognize applications he has yet to consider.
"We want to work with experts at WashU Medicine and elsewhere to explore the possibilities," Ke said. "Hopefully this paper will help us get the word out to researchers and potential investors."

So far, Ke and his team have produced the material in small quantities, just tens of grams at a time. But with the concept successfully demonstrated, they believe production could scale up to meet demand.

articles.title: Dropping degree requirements linked to higher pay for workers without degrees
articles.dek: The requirements set by human resources (HR) greatly influence the professional opportunities available to different segments of the population.
paragraphs: The requirements set by human resources (HR) greatly influence the professional opportunities available to different segments of the population. For instance, if a job requires applicants to have earned a bachelor's or master's degree in a relevant subject, people without them may be excluded from the selection process, even if they have gained relevant skills through experience or professional training.

Some employers in the United States and other countries have been removing degree requirements from job postings. These interventions are often part of an approach described as "skills-based" hiring, which places greater emphasis on the experiences and abilities of applicants than on their academic background.

Researchers at the University of Kentucky, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) recently set out to explore the possible impact of removing degree requirements for jobs by analyzing online job postings, along with associated employment and earnings records. Their findings, published in Nature Human Behaviour , suggest that workers in the U. S. without four-year college degrees hired into jobs that had dropped degree requirements earned more than comparable workers starting jobs that had never required one.

The researchers analyzed a large pool of data gathered by Lightcast, a company that records online job advertisements, and by the U. S. Census Bureau. This included job postings collected by Lightcast and U. S. Census Bureau employment records related to approximately 446,500 job starts in the U. S. between 2011 and 2021.

Firstly, the team tried to determine whether degree requirements had changed in the U. S. and whether this may have benefited people without degrees. In particular, they looked at whether a reduction in degree requirements was linked to a greater number of people without degrees being hired or differences in the starting pay these workers received.

"Matching job postings to 446,500 job starts in U. S. administrative data from 2011 to 2021, we show that employers reduced the share of postings requiring a degree by more than 10%," wrote Thomas Lyttelton, Dylan K. Nelson and Nathan Wilmers in their paper.

The researchers found that workers without four-year degrees hired into jobs that dropped degree requirements earned approximately $4,600 more annually than workers with similar academic backgrounds hired for jobs that never required a degree. This advantage in earnings appeared to persist for at least five years.

Lyttelton and his colleagues also found that the workers without four-year degrees hired into jobs that dropped degree requirements were more likely to be Black, Hispanic or women than the workers they replaced. While removing degree requirements was found to have some social benefits, the team's analyses suggest that many employers still hired graduates for jobs that no longer listed degrees as required.

The findings of this study highlight the potential advantages of removing degree requirements from job postings, suggesting that it could give workers without four-year college degrees access to better-paid jobs. Moreover, changing degree requirements during the hiring process could be beneficial for the recruiting organizations.

"Employers also benefit, as removing degree requirements reduces labor costs," wrote Lyttelton, Nelson and Wilmers. "Yet most employers that drop requirements do not hire non-college workers (non-college hiring rises 1. 2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, (0. 5, 2. 0)). Decredentialing is a promising tool for social mobility, but only when employers follow through."

In the future, the insights gathered by the authors could inspire more organizations to drop degree requirements. For such interventions to effectively broaden the opportunities available to less educated workers, however, companies need to commit to them and be prepared to actually select people without a degree.

articles.title: 1,000-Year-Old Welsh Legend May Have Revealed the Location of a Lost Roman Fortress
articles.dek: A medieval Welsh legend may have preserved the location of a real Roman fort, raising the possibility that other ancient stories contain forgotten pieces of history.
paragraphs: A medieval Welsh legend may have preserved the location of a real Roman fort, raising the possibility that other ancient stories contain forgotten pieces of history.
The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, southwest Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus.

The site is mentioned in Breuddwyd Macsen Wledig (The Dream of Macsen Wledig), a story about a Roman emperor who travels to Wales. Until now, the account of a camp in that location had largely been treated as a product of medieval imagination. But the archaeological discovery raises an intriguing question: can ancient stories preserve memories of places and events that have been lost to history?

The Dream of Macsen Wledig is one of the 11 medieval Welsh-language tales traditionally grouped together as the Mabinogion . These tales blend history, folklore, magic, and legend, while some people see in them lost myths. Featuring kings, warriors, magicians, and supernatural beings, the stories offer a glimpse into how people in medieval Wales understood their past and the world around them.

The tales survive in two important Welsh-language manuscripts: Llyfr Gwyn Rhydderch (the White Book of Rhydderch), compiled around the mid-14th century, and Llyfr Coch Hergest (the Red Book of Hergest), written toward the end of that century.
But the stories themselves are older. They had been transmitted and copied since before King Edward I’s conquest of Wales in 1282, and perhaps as early as the 11th century.

Five of the tales feature Arthur, the legendary warrior whose tales spread throughout all of Europe. The Four Branches of the Mabinogi are a group of stories spanning the landscapes of Wales, Ireland and England, of this world and the supernatural otherworld. The remaining two, including The Dream of Macsen Wledig, reshape particular strands of early British history through native storytelling. All the tales offer imaginative accounts of power and political authority.

In The Dream of Macsen Wledig, a Roman emperor falls in love with a woman he sees in a dream. Determined to find her, he sends messengers to follow the route he has dreamed of. Their journey takes them across Europe and eventually to what is now Caernarfon, in northwest Wales.

The emperor is called Macsen Wledig (Macsen the Leader). His character is a literary composite of a number of historical characters, most notably the Galician Magnus Maximus, a Roman general who became Emperor in the late 4th century. Born in a province that is now part of Spain and Portugal, Magnus Maximus seized power in Britain and went on to rule much of the western Roman Empire, including Gaul (roughly modern France and neighboring regions).

His legacy in Wales is particularly significant. In the popular Welsh song Yma o Hyd (Still Here), first released in 1983, the singer and former politician Dafydd Iwan invokes Magnus Maximus’s departure from Britain, supposedly leaving Wales behind as an entire nation.
The song draws on a powerful literary tradition – that the departure of Rome from Britain, just before the arrival of the English, saw the birth of Welsh identity.

But the medieval story is not a straightforward account of historical events. Like the song, it blends historical memory with imagination. Its importance lies not simply in whether every detail is factually accurate, but in what the story tells us about how Welsh people understood the past.

The woman in Macsen’s dream is Elen Luyddog (Elen of the Hosts). She is also a composite character, associated with two figures named Helen or Helena – Helen of Caernarfon and Helena of Constantinople, mother of Constantine the Great. Both were 4th-century saints.

In the story, Elen insists that Macsen travel to Wales to marry her. He agrees, and she becomes empress. Her father is appointed Viceroy of Britain, and together they begin building powerful fortresses. Elen asks Macsen to establish three towns: Caerllion (Caerleon), Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen) and Caernarfon.

articles.title: Scientists Finally Solve the 1,700-Year-Old Mystery of 8,000 Dead Frogs
articles.dek: Forests cleared for livestock in Roman Britain may have made young frogs more vulnerable to owls, revealing how human activity shaped wildlife nearly 1,700 years ago.
paragraphs: Forests cleared for livestock in Roman Britain may have made young frogs more vulnerable to owls, revealing how human activity shaped wildlife nearly 1,700 years ago.

Finding 8,000 frog bones buried in a single ditch raised a strange question for archaeologists working along England’s A14 highway. What had killed so many frogs, and why had their remains accumulated in one place? Evidence that the ditch filled within just one year made the discovery even more puzzling.

Nearly a decade later, researchers from Bournemouth University and Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) believe they have identified the culprits. The frogs were likely eaten by birds of prey, particularly short-eared owls and hen harriers, that took advantage of a landscape transformed by human activity during the Roman period.

The bones were uncovered between 2016 and 2018 during the National Highways A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme. After learning about the discovery through news reports, Dr. Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth University contacted Dr. Vicki Ewens, a senior zooarchaeologist at MOLA, to investigate.

Clarkson compared damage on the ancient bones with patterns documented in previous studies and found evidence that the frogs had been eaten by birds of prey. Although this helped identify the likely predators, it did not fully explain how so many remains had collected in such a short time.

A closer examination of the frogs’ ages offered another clue. Using a pioneering method based on measuring their humeri, or upper arm bones, the researchers determined that most had died young, during the winter of their first year of life. Radiocarbon dating conducted by the University of Vienna placed the remains approximately 1,700 years ago, during the Roman period.

At the time, Fen waters were retreating from the valley, creating favorable conditions for frogs to breed. This would have provided a plentiful food source for birds hunting in the area. Changes to the surrounding landscape may have made the young frogs even more vulnerable.

Short-eared owls typically hunt over grassland, yet the valley had been wooded during the Iron Age. To understand how the environment changed, researchers examined evidence from snails, pollen, and charcoal. Their findings showed that substantial areas of woodland had gradually been cleared to create grazing land for livestock.
By the Roman period, large stretches of open ground had replaced much of the woodland. With fewer trees providing cover, frogs would have been more exposed to predators hunting across the grassland.
“We don’t often get an owl’s-eye view of what it was like in the past from archaeological sites,” said Clarkson, who led the study.

“The mystery of these frogs has been solved – a feast of frogs that were eaten and their bones left behind by a group of owls. These bones not only tell us about life for people living near the Roman Fens, but they also give insights into the natural world – what wild animals were getting up to in the past, and what life was like for them,” he added.

The findings may also offer clues about how people used the valley during Roman times. Researchers suggest that communities may have visited the area seasonally to move livestock between grazing pastures. A less crowded landscape could have provided favorable conditions for hunting birds, although this connection remains a possible explanation rather than a confirmed finding.
What began as an unusual collection of animal remains has therefore helped researchers reconstruct both the changing environment and the activities of people who lived near the Roman Fens.

As Ewens concludes, “I had so many theories as to why such a large collection of frog bones was recovered from this small feature. It’s been great to collaborate with Paul to finally answer this question. This research shows how even the smallest animal recovered on a site can help us to understand not only past environmental conditions but human activity within a wider landscape.”

articles.title: Scientists Discover Bizarre Deep-Sea Creature That Survives Without Most of Its Digestive System
articles.dek: An unusual sea creature survives with much of its digestive system missing, thanks to a remarkable partnership with bacteria that could offer new clues about how life evolves.
paragraphs: An unusual sea creature survives with much of its digestive system missing, thanks to a remarkable partnership with bacteria that could offer new clues about how life evolves.

Deep beneath the seafloor, where sunlight never reaches and oxygen is almost nonexistent, scientists have discovered an unusual relationship that may help explain how marine life survives in some of Earth’s most extreme environments. A deep-sea mollusk living in the South China Sea contains a previously unknown cellular structure packed with bacteria, offering new clues about how animals adapt to conditions that would be inhospitable to most other species.

The discovery adds to a growing understanding of cold seep ecosystems, where life depends on chemical energy rather than sunlight. These environments contain abundant methane and hydrogen sulfide, which certain bacteria can use to support their metabolism. Animals such as deep-sea mussels, clams, and tubeworms have evolved close relationships with these microbes, providing them with shelter inside their cells in exchange for nutrients.
Until now, however, scientists had found no clear evidence that animals could develop specialized organelles dedicated to maintaining these bacterial partnerships.

The new research centers on Chaetoderma shenloong , also known as the Divine Dragon Glistenworm. This unusual mollusk belongs to the aplacophoran class Caudofoveata and can grow to more than 150 millimeters (nearly 6 inches) long, far larger than most of its relatives. Its distinctive characteristics earned it recognition as one of the “Top-Ten Marine Species of 2024.”

Researchers found that the animal spends much of its life buried tens of centimeters beneath the seafloor, in sediment rich in hydrogen sulfide and containing almost no oxygen. Understanding how it survives there led the team to examine an unexpected feature of its anatomy.

Using anatomical analysis, micro-computed tomography, and three-dimensional imaging, the scientists discovered that Chaetoderma shenloong has a digestive system unlike those of most mollusks. Its radula, a feeding structure commonly used by mollusks, is heavily reduced, while its midgut, hindgut, and anus have almost completely disappeared.

Instead, an extensive system of digestive glands occupies most of its body cavity. These glands contain enormous numbers of symbiotic bacteria that serve as the animal’s primary source of nutrients and energy.
Closer examination revealed something even more unusual inside the glands.

The bacteria were concentrated within spherical structures measuring approximately 10 to 15 micrometers across. Each structure was enclosed by more than 20 layers of membrane and contained hundreds to thousands of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria. The researchers named this structure the dracosphera , Latin for “dragon ball,” because of its beadlike shape and surrounding layers.

A single host cell accommodated more than 1,600 bacterial symbionts on average. The dracosphera also lacked familiar cellular components, including host nuclei and lysosomes, distinguishing it from an ordinary cell or a typical digestive compartment.

This arrangement suggests that the mollusk may have developed a specialized structure for housing and maintaining its bacterial partners, potentially representing a previously unrecognized form of cooperation between animals and microorganisms.
The scientists then investigated how this relationship might function in an environment where oxygen is so scarce.

Genomic analyses of Chaetoderma shenloong and its symbiotic bacteria revealed that the microbes possess adaptations allowing them to maintain their metabolism with very little oxygen. The mollusk, meanwhile, lives deep in the sediment to obtain chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide that its bacterial partners can use.

articles.title: Babies in ancient Greek colony started solid food at 3 months but nursed for nearly 4 years, chemical signatures suggest
articles.dek: Over 2,500 years ago, Himera was a Greek colony inhabited by local Sicilians, Phoenicians and Greeks.
paragraphs: Over 2,500 years ago, Himera was a Greek colony inhabited by local Sicilians, Phoenicians and Greeks. Despite their diverse cultural backgrounds, they all shared one thing: they began weaning their babies early and continued for a long time.

A new study published in the European Journal of Archaeology analyzed the chemical signatures in Himera children's bones and found that babies began eating solid foods at just 3 months but were not fully weaned until around 3. 8 years old. That's much longer than ancient writers suggested and sheds light on how mothers in a diverse society like Himera approached child care.
Laurie Reitsema, a biological anthropologist at the University of Georgia and a mother herself, said, "It was exciting to see 2,500-year-old evidence of mothers' responsiveness to infant needs."

Himera was an ancient Greek outpost located in Sicily between the seventh and fifth centuries B. C. , the study authors wrote. It was founded by Dorian and Chalcidian colonists before growing into a large city home to a diverse multicultural population.
According to the study, archaeologists have uncovered over 13,000 burials. Many of these are of adults. Infant and child mortality appeared to be surprisingly low.

Children born into such a diverse world likely experienced different cultural realities than their parents and would become the seeds of cultural change across generations, the study reported. However, what these childhoods may have looked like remains unclear.

Weaning is one crucial cultural and biological milestone every child experiences. To better understand how that practice played out in the ancient city of Himera, Reitsema and her colleagues looked at the carbon and nitrogen chemical signatures preserved in some of its inhabitants' bones.

Nitrogen told them how long a baby was breastfed, because its values rise during nursing until a baby's chemical signature looks like a carnivore's. Carbon told them what plant-based solid foods babies ate once they stopped drinking only milk.
"Breastfed babies look different than weaned babies, isotopically, because their diets consist of milk, which differs isotopically from other foods (babies are top carnivores! )," Reitsema said.

According to the study, the team examined 58 children's and 27 adult women's bones. What they found was that children at Himera began weaning early, around 3 months, around 2 to 3 months earlier than ancient physicians like Galen and Soranus recommended.

Meanwhile, breastfeeding continued far longer than in most modern preindustrial societies, for around 3. 8 years. Soranus recommended weaning at just 1. 5 years, and Galen suggested breastfeeding should stop at 3 years.
The study suggests this long period of breastfeeding may explain why Himera's infant mortality was so low.
"Breastfeeding is well known to support infant survival," Reitsema said, "especially in places without reliable access to clean, safe drinking water, which describes most of human history."

On the other hand, the study focused on children who died young, despite being breastfed for years. "Would a baby with an optimal weaning trajectory be dying at age 2 or 3?" Reitsema asked. "It's possible that the weaning behaviors we see in this study reflect a specifically unsuccessful strategy."

articles.title: An ancient failed rift is reawakening inside one of Africa's oldest landmasses
articles.dek: In April 2017, a magnitude 6. 5 earthquake shook southern Africa from an unlikely place: the middle of the Kalahari Craton in eastern Botswana.
paragraphs: In April 2017, a magnitude 6. 5 earthquake shook southern Africa from an unlikely place: the middle of the Kalahari Craton in eastern Botswana. Cratons are the ancient cores of continents, and this one is built from blocks of crust up to 3. 7 billion years old. Geologists have long considered such regions too cold, too thick and too rigid to tear apart.

Now, a new study led by researchers at the Botswana International University of Science and Technology (BIUST) and the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory shows that the craton is indeed being pulled apart. It also shows that the rift doing the pulling has tried this before. The findings are published in the journal Tectonics . The work challenges long-held assumptions about continental stability, revealing how ancient geological seams can reactivate to fracture even the oldest continental cores.

"The earthquake happened in the middle of the craton, a region where no one expected to have an active fault slipping, let alone an active plate boundary developing," says co-author Folarin Kolawole. He is a structural geologist at Lamont and an assistant professor in the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences within the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

The new rift lies at the far southern tip of the East African Rift System, where the African continent is slowly stretching apart. Rifts like these are the earliest stage of a divergent plate boundary, the kind that splits a continent and opens a new ocean if successful. For decades, scientists thought the southern end of this system lay in the Okavango Rift Zone of northern Botswana, first identified in the 1970s by Lamont geologist Christopher Scholz and colleagues. Studies of the 2017 earthquake revealed that it reaches nearly 200 miles (320 kilometers) farther, into the craton itself.

This is a surprise, considering how rifts usually go around cratons rather than through them. Around the world, continental rifts tend to follow mountain belts—the younger and weaker zones where ancient cratons once collided. Only a handful of rifts, such as the one that opened the Labrador Sea between Canada and Greenland, are known to have broken across a craton. "It's counterintuitive," Kolawole says. "It basically challenges age-old thinking."
"Whether rifts do propagate through cratons has been a really big question in geoscience," says the study's lead author, Boniface Kgosidintsi of BIUST.

To understand how the rift is breaking into the craton, the team focused on the Khurutshe Fault, which cuts a 50-mile-long (80-kilometer-long) scarp, or step, across the flat Kalahari landscape about 50 miles (80 kilometers) south of the 2017 earthquake. In places, the land on one side of the fault sits as much as 400 feet (120 meters) higher than the other.

The researchers dug trenches across the scarp alongside Botswana's A1 highway and examined deeper excavations dug for a government water pipeline. They imaged the rock below with electrical resistivity tomography , which Kolawole likens to a CAT scan of the fault. And they analyzed records from 20 groundwater boreholes drilled across the area.

All three lines of evidence told the same story. When a fault slips, the land on one side drops, and sediment piles up in the low spot, forming a wedge that thickens toward the fault. The team found that both the modern Kalahari Desert sands and much older rock layers from the Jurassic period form such wedges against the same fault. That means the fault was moving in the Jurassic, roughly 180 million years ago, and is moving again today.

The trenches the researchers dug revealed more details about the fault's past. Beneath reddish-brown, windblown Kalahari sand, the team hit hard, highly cemented Jurassic sandstone shot through with white veins of calcite, "a spider web network of whitish lines through the rocks," Kolawole says. The calcite was deposited by hot fluids, like those that build mineral terraces at Yellowstone's hot springs, rising through cracks opened by the fault. Some rock surfaces were polished and scored by slip along the fault.

articles.title: Army’s plan to blow up aging explosives will spread lead over part of Iowa – what you need to know about the risks
articles.dek: The U. S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice .
paragraphs: The U. S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice . According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing lead azide , an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “ unacceptable risk of accidental detonation .” Intentionally detonating the barrels is considered the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined.

However, the explosions are expected to release a large plume of lead particles, and lead is a neurotoxin. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, a town of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa. People and farms would be in the path of the plume as the wind blows it for miles.

The detonations were briefly delayed by the backlash and rescheduled for Nov. 23, 2026 . And a federal appeals court separately paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit for the detonations after two groups sued. It wasn’t immediately clear if the plan would be delayed again. The Justice Department argues that the permit isn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat.

With all the concern, we asked Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, about the risks people in the region would face. O'Shaughnessy is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan.

If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets .

Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The big concern there is for young children . If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.

Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies , including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to hide out in bones and teeth , where it can leach out and cause harm.

Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body . That’s a pretty strong statement.
Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.

We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.

In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.

If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.

If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan on Nov. 23 , the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southeast. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead as it slowly floats by.
That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.
Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a list of precautions that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.

The Army is advising people near the plant to vacate their homes during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.
Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.

After the plumed dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.

Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some dairy farmers are concerned about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.
Our results from sampling during and after the plume should help people better understand the risks.

My colleagues and I will be looking at two aspects of potential exposure to lead: the airborne dust, which we’ll collect with instruments during the plume to get the lead concentration, and then dust that settles on surfaces and the ground, which we’ll collect with gauzelike pads and send to a lab for analysis.
The lab will be able to tell how much lead is in those samples, and the air samples will let us calculate how much people were exposed to the lead.

This is all happening last minute – we only found out about the plan a few days before the Army initially planned to detonate the barrels. Thankfully, the university and our federal- and state-funded centers have the people and technology to quickly carry out testing. We hope to have results about a week after it happens. The U. S. Environmental Protection Agency also has a team that will be doing sampling.

articles.title: Cerebral Palsy May Not Be What Scientists Thought It Was
articles.dek: New research is challenging how scientists understand cerebral palsy (CP).
paragraphs: New research is challenging how scientists understand cerebral palsy (CP). Of 515 genes previously linked to the condition, only 89 showed a statistically significant association in a new study, suggesting that many proposed genetic connections still lack sufficient evidence.

Published in the journal American Journal of Human Genetics , the research also proposes a different way to classify CP. Rather than treating it as a single disorder, the scientists suggest it may be better understood as a collection of symptoms arising from multiple underlying conditions.

Cerebral palsy is the most common motor disability in children, with up to 10,000 babies diagnosed in the United States annually. It has traditionally been associated with complications around birth, including premature delivery and temporary oxygen deprivation. However, genetic research over the past decade has increasingly pointed to inherited or newly occurring genetic variants as potential contributors. Unlike progressive neurological diseases, CP does not worsen over time, and rehabilitation and physical therapy can improve symptoms.

“There has been a lack of consensus on the definition of cerebral palsy and on the role of genetics in disease pathogenesis, leading to substantial variability in whether a child is diagnosed with CP,” says corresponding author Peter Robinson of the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine and the Berlin Institute of Health at Charité.

“We have developed a paradigm that considers CP to be a phenotypic trait rather than a precise disease diagnosis. A better understanding of specific genetic variants has the potential to improve our understanding of the biology of the disease.”

To investigate the genetic basis of CP, the researchers evaluated evidence from 21 previously published studies involving 5,440 people diagnosed with the condition. These studies had identified potentially causal variants across hundreds of genes, but the new statistical analysis found convincing evidence of association for only a fraction of them.

“We decided to do this study because there has been no accepted statistical method to determine if a disease-associated gene is truly linked to CP,” says first author Adam Arterbery of the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine. “We discovered it was extremely difficult to find statistical evidence of causality for many of the genetic variants previously linked to CP.”

The team also performed whole-genome sequencing on 460 children from 453 families receiving care at Shriners Children’s hospitals across the United States. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic genetic variants were identified in 70 families, spanning 60 genes. However, just 16 of those genes overlapped with the genes supported by statistically significant evidence in the analysis of earlier studies.

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not disprove connections between CP and the remaining genes. Instead, the available data are insufficient to establish those associations with statistical confidence. They propose viewing CP as a clinical characteristic that can emerge from different genetic disorders and environmental influences, rather than a single disease with a common biological origin.

“This framework could improve interpretation of genomic testing, help identify children who may warrant closer CP surveillance or specialist referral, and potentially identify genetic conditions requiring disease-specific management,” Robinson says. “But clinical utility and patient benefit will absolutely need validation before these findings can be applied to patient care.”

Future studies will focus on larger patient populations, prospective evaluations of clinical benefits and costs, and better access to genomic and medical data. “We hope our study will stimulate discussion about CP terminology, gene-disease associations, and variant interpretation,” Arterbery says. “The most productive response will be further validation and development of better genotype-phenotype evidence rather than treating the findings as a definitive list of CP genes.”

This work was supported by Shriners Children’s, the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, the National Human Genome Research Institute, and the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation.

articles.title: Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'
articles.dek: Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot.
paragraphs: Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We've always had trouble measuring them in the "megaelectronvolt" (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the "MeV gap." But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series , takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20–200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

The "gap" comes from a technological blind spot. Scientists have plenty of tools in the lower-energy spectra, such as the Chandra X-ray Observatory, that can capture radiation at the X-ray end of the electromagnetic spectrum. They also have a great number of tools at the high end of gamma-ray spectroscopy, including the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which is capable of finding higher-energy gamma rays.

But why are low-energy gamma rays so hard to catch? Gamma rays notoriously pass right through mirrors and every other attempt to reflect them. Telescopes like Fermi-LAT can be thought of more as particle detectors in orbit than traditional telescopes. They track what happens when a gamma-ray photon hits layers of tungsten and silicon inside their chassis.

At high energies—around 1 gigaelectronvolt (GeV)—the damage done to those layers is catastrophic enough to be able to trace a line back to a source. However, in the lower 20–200 MeV range, the photons scatter much more randomly, making it difficult to track where precisely they came from.

Fermi-LAT is only capable of tracking a single 20 MeV photon to a patch of the sky about 20 degrees wide—more than 40 times the size of the full moon. Combine that with a massive amount of background radiation caused by everything from the sun to distant galaxies, and it can be a real pain to pick out the direction of any one particular source.

However, Fermi-LAT has been operating now for almost two decades, and with that much data, there's some math that can help. The researchers combined 14 years' worth of collected data with some advanced statistical modeling techniques to pinpoint 450 distinct gamma-ray sources, cataloged in what they are calling the Second Catalog of Low-Energy Fermi-LAT Sources, or 2FLE. Cross-checking them with other radio, optical and X-ray data showed known counterparts for 377 of those objects.

The vast majority of those objects—325 of them—are far outside the Milky Way. Almost half of the entire group of objects consists of flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), a very extreme type of active galactic nucleus. FSRQs represent a type of "blazar"—a supermassive black hole that is pointing one of its twin jets of plasma directly at Earth. The 2FLE catalog confirms that FSRQ blazars pump out the majority of their energy in this 20–200 MeV spectral window.

Closer to home, the catalog includes 52 sources from inside the Milky Way. Most of them are pulsars—the spinning leftovers left behind when a supermassive star explodes into a supernova. But one intriguing outlier was gamma rays that appear to be coming from M2, a globular cluster, which would mark the first time it's ever been observed at gamma-ray energies.

Perhaps the most intriguing part of the paper, though, is the 73 sources that don't have a clear counterpart at other energies. Sixty of those appear to be brand-new gamma-ray discoveries. And while some of those signals might turn out to be overlapping signals from neighboring objects, it's likely there are at least some truly new exotic cosmic accelerators in the data set awaiting follow-up observations.

One particular mystery source seems to align with an object called 2FLE J0340. 8+5258, which seems to also have been detected by an observatory in China and appears to be capable of generating light across nine orders of magnitude in energy.

Fermi-LAT itself seems to have reached its limit with this new data set. The researchers have likely squeezed everything they could out of the decades of data from this satellite, which was originally launched in 2008.

articles.title: A Major Review Reveals Three Antidepressants That May Outperform Prozac
articles.dek: A massive review of 30,000 people suggests three antidepressants may outperform Prozac, but the findings reveal how much remains unknown about long-term depression treatment.
paragraphs: A massive review of 30,000 people suggests three antidepressants may outperform Prozac, but the findings reveal how much remains unknown about long-term depression treatment.
A new review has found that some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found that people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta), and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.
Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

Treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.
In 2024-2025, 3. 8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant .
For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce , and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants, so it’s important this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Studies of real-world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.
Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

The new review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.
They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.
People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

articles.title: New Once-Daily Pill Slashes Bad Cholesterol by Nearly 65% in Clinical Trial
articles.dek: A pill taken before breakfast cut “bad” cholesterol by nearly two-thirds in a trial of people already taking statins.
paragraphs: A pill taken before breakfast cut “bad” cholesterol by nearly two-thirds in a trial of people already taking statins.

High cholesterol can silently damage blood vessels for decades, increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes without causing noticeable symptoms. Much of that danger comes from excess LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, which contributes to fatty plaque buildup inside artery walls. Although statins help millions of people control their cholesterol, some patients need additional treatment to bring their levels down.

A newly approved once-daily pill could provide another option. Lipfendra (enlicitide) reduced LDL cholesterol by nearly 65% in a clinical trial involving adults already taking statins. Approved by the FDA on July 16, 2026, it is the first oral medication in a powerful class of cholesterol treatments previously available only through injections.

Enlicitide targets PCSK9, a protein that influences how efficiently the liver removes LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream. Normally, PCSK9 promotes the destruction of LDL receptors on liver cells. When these receptors are lost, the liver becomes less effective at clearing circulating cholesterol.

By blocking PCSK9, enlicitide allows more LDL receptors to remain active, helping the liver remove additional cholesterol from the blood. Unlike earlier PCSK9 inhibitors that require injections, enlicitide uses a specialized macrocyclic peptide formulation with absorption-enhancing ingredients, allowing the medication to be taken orally.

A review published in Annals of Pharmacotherapy found that enlicitide reduced LDL cholesterol by 57. 1% to 64. 6% after 24 weeks across clinical trials. These reductions were comparable to those achieved with injectable PCSK9 inhibitors.

In a direct comparison involving patients already taking statins, LDL cholesterol fell by approximately 65% with enlicitide. By comparison, reductions were about 28% with ezetimibe and 6% with bempedoic acid, two other oral medications used to manage high cholesterol.

The review examined research identified through PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane through July 17, 2026. Participants included adults with elevated cholesterol and those with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, an inherited condition that causes unusually high LDL cholesterol levels from birth and increases the risk of premature cardiovascular disease.

In the largest trial, adverse effects occurred at similar rates among participants receiving enlicitide and those taking a placebo. However, a separate study involving people with inherited high cholesterol reported more diarrhea and dizziness among those receiving the medication. Longer-term monitoring will help establish its safety with continued use.

Enlicitide must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach. Patients may drink water, black coffee, or plain tea with the medication but must wait at least 30 minutes before consuming food or other beverages. A 30-day supply carries a list price of $315, although actual costs depend on insurance coverage.

While clinical trials have established that enlicitide substantially reduces LDL cholesterol, researchers have not yet determined whether it also prevents heart attacks and strokes. An ongoing cardiovascular outcomes trial is investigating whether its cholesterol-lowering effects translate into fewer serious cardiovascular events.

articles.title: From screens in class to smart glasses, Norway rethinks new technologies
articles.dek: Three years ago, a schoolteacher in Norway was reprimanded for putting his pupils' iPads aside to return to pen and paper.
paragraphs: Three years ago, a schoolteacher in Norway was reprimanded for putting his pupils' iPads aside to return to pen and paper. Now, the whole country is rethinking its approach to new technologies.
After making laptops and screens ubiquitous in schools across the country, Norway is bringing back textbooks in a bid to reverse a sharp decline in pupils' reading and writing skills.
The desire to regain control over technology, rather than just accept the consequences that come with it, extends beyond the school environment in the tech-loving country.

"There is reason to believe that the introduction of screens in schools happened too quickly, before we had sufficient knowledge about their effects and about what constitutes good pedagogical use of digital devices," Norway's Digitalization Minister Torgeir Micaelsen told AFP.
For nearly 20 years, Norway has been pushing computers and tablets in classrooms, a trend further reinforced during COVID.
Starting in 2023, primary schools in Oslo were even supposed to equip every pupil with a digital device.

Third-grade teacher Pal Ludvig Finstad broke with the prevailing regulations one day, deciding to temporarily put tablets away in favor of paper and pencils to help his pupils who were struggling with reading and writing.
"My pedagogical assessment was that, at that point, the pupils needed a new approach, and that it was urgent," he told the newspaper Klassekampen in 2024.
He ended up getting a written warning from the school administration.
Ironically, Oslo municipality has just dropped its requirement for one device per pupil in primary schools, giving schools more leeway in choosing their teaching tools.
"The screen itself is not the problem. It's the way it's used, when the tool becomes more important than the content," primary school principal Silje Ween told AFP.
"Just as a book is a useful and absolutely necessary tool, an iPad can be as well, but one does not exclude the other," she noted.
Norwegian authorities have, in turn, recommended regulating the use of cellphones in schools and introducing artificial intelligence into the school curriculum only gradually.
The government is also seeking to enshrine access to printed textbooks in law.

articles.title: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation
articles.dek: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.
paragraphs: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U. S. space economy.

NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed funding.

This early-stage research and development work will tackle an array of topics, including those related to Artemis and the establishment of a U. S. Moon Base . Selected projects include next-generation battery solutions, robotic systems with sensing capabilities for the extreme lunar environment, and tools to prepare for construction of critical infrastructure, such as lunar landing pads.

NASA’s SBIR/STTR program provides support for entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses to advance and commercialize technologies that can advance the agency’s missions. Working with the program, a company’s path toward commercialization or infusion into NASA missions occurs in phases. The latest awards involved two of these phases.

The new Phase I contracts will receive up to $225,000 each to establish the merit and feasibility of their proposed innovation. A portion of the projects selected are STTR awards, provided to small businesses partnered with research institutions.

The Phase II awards, with 98 contracts valued at up to $1. 3 million each, will continue work begun in Phase I projects selected in 2025, targeting demonstration and delivery of the innovative technologies.
Following are a few examples of research supported through these recent awards:

An SBIR Phase II award for Opterus Research and Development Inc. supports a project focused on bringing power to the surface of the Moon and Mars by developing a modular system of rollable solar arrays. The arrays can be handled robotically, are compatible with various support structures, and work even in dusty surface conditions. The technology could be scaled up to 50 kilowatts, and it could provide a reliable power source to help both NASA and commercial space companies develop infrastructure on the Moon .

This SBIR Phase I award, led by Intelligent Fiber Optic Systems Corporation, aims to help lunar rovers perform complex tasks independently on the Moon. The firm’s 10-foot, extendable robotic arm can both “see” and has a sense of touch, combining a camera with sensors to detect and measure surface textures, contact forces, and temperature. The technology could help automate many lunar surface tasks, such as cleaning solar panels, positioning habitat structures, and collecting scientific samples from hard-to-reach locations. On Earth, the same instrumented robotic arms could be used to inspect and repair power lines, nuclear reactors, or other infrastructure in hazardous environments.

Elementium Materials Inc. , selected for an SBIR Phase I award, is developing an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module for space applications and cold-climate uses on Earth. The technology can operate down to minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit without active heating, reducing the need for heaters and insulating layers to work on the Moon. With the space and mass that’s saved, NASA missions can launch other tools and science experiments, instead. This battery technology could help keep rovers, habitats, and other infrastructure running through the frigid, 14-day lunar night and potentially on Mars.

A collaboration between Slate Geotechnical Consultants Inc. and the Colorado School of Mines will evaluate two approaches to preparing lunar regolith for repeated lunar landings, so that routine mission activities can have sturdy, reusable landing pads. Without such pads, the force generated by a rocket can blast out loose, gravel-like regolith from the surface, throw up dust, or create craters, potentially damaging spacecraft and nearby infrastructure. The project, supported by an STTR Phase I award, will also investigate ways to use rovers to repair and maintain future lunar landing pads.
Complete lists of the selected proposals are available on the SBIR/STTR program’s website:
NASA’s SBIR/STTR program is part of the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate and is managed by NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley.

articles.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
articles.dek: “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people .
paragraphs: “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people .

The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister.
“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains.

I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.
One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes.
My sister was one of 43. 5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults.

The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion .

Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price.
Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people.

That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.”

Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 .
But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones.
Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits.
Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one.

AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.

Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax.

Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability.

Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives.
But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing.

Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.
Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party.

articles.title: NASA Honor Awards Ceremony Recognizes Employees at Stennis Space Center
articles.dek: Employees contributing to NASA’s mission at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, were recognized during the center’s Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18.
paragraphs: Employees contributing to NASA’s mission at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, were recognized during the center’s Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18.

Presenting the awards were Christine Powell, NASA Stennis center director, and Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager responsible for management and oversight of NASA’s initiative to return humans to the Moon.

Stephen Rawls of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Center Director’s Excellence Award for exceptional leadership and technical excellence in advancing NASA Stennis propulsion testing capabilities for critical NASA and commercial programs.

Bradley Tyree of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Engineering Excellence Award for engineering excellence and contributions to the successful testing of the Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment Confined by Missile Program.

Anna Lizana of Diamondhead, Mississippi, received the Excellence in Customer Service Award for exceptional environmental compliance support that advanced commercial partnerships, streamlined agency processes, and reduced regulatory risk.

Daniel Jones of Huntsville, Alabama, received the Excellence in Innovation Award for the invention of the Hydrocarbon Propellants Enabling Reproduction of Flows in Rocket Engines, a system for low-cost aerodynamic data acquisition.

Peyton Pinson of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Leadership Excellence Award for exceptional leadership as E-1 test director, providing steady guidance and strengthening team cohesion throughout a demanding and high-tempo year of propulsion testing.

Joseph Schuyler of Pass Christian, Mississippi, received the J. Harry Guin Leadership Award for transformative leadership that advanced NASA Stennis propulsion testing capability and strengthened its role as the agency’s Center of Excellence in Propulsion Testing.

Michael McDaniel of Slidell, Louisiana, received the Roy S. Estess Service Leadership Award for exceptional partnership, sustained leadership, and an unwavering commitment to his community as the general manager of L3Harris Technologies at NASA Stennis that embodies the legacy of the late center director.

Amer Arshad of Diamondhead, Mississippi, received the Space Flight Awareness Trailblazer Award for innovative leadership, system stewardship, and collaborative solutions that have strengthened NASA’s mission through improved reliability, insight, and efficiency.

Claire O’Shaughnessy of Mandeville, Louisiana, received the Space Flight Awareness Trailblazer Award for innovative leadership and collaborative drive that strengthened the center’s mission by advancing critical facility capabilities for the agency’s Artemis program.

In addition to individual awards, the Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment, Confined by Missile Test Team received the Space Flight Awareness Team Award for exceptional technical achievement in executing a test series that has provided mission critical safety data for the future of human spaceflight.

Briou Bourgeois accepted the award on behalf of the team, which included: Chase Aubry, Brandon Carver, Jack Conley, James Connell, Armando Delgado, Mateo Ferreira, Pau Fuller, Mark Hancock, Steven Helmstetter, Paula Hensarling, Jason Hopper, Chase Lemaire, Addison Mitchell, Randall Pigott, Stephen Rawls, Skip Roberts, Mark Robinson, Luke Roger, Matthew Sappington, Robert Simmers, Jason Richard, Bradley Tyree, Richard Wear, and Robert Williams.

The ceremony also honored employees who reached significant milestone anniversaries in their civil service careers. Employees with 40 years of service were Curtis Armstrong, Jason Edge, and Kevin Power. Employees with 35 years of service were Michael Brashear, Reginald Ellis II, Arlen Griffey, Bradley Messer, Christine Powell, and Michael Rewis. Skip Roberts was recognized for 30 years of service.
